units.text: 2. Ground beetles were sampled by pitfall trapping in 40 poplar forest stands (sampling plots) along the Irtysh River in Northwestern China. We investigated responses of carabid activity density, species diversity and functional diversity (FD) to stand characteristics and surrounding landscape structure (the overall diversity and percentage cover of vegetation productivity classes in the surrounding area of each sampling plot based on normalised difference vegetation index). 3. While carabid activity density only responded positively to the overall diversity of vegetation productivity classes, carabid species diversity was positively associated with this landscape factor as well as vegetation cover but negatively associated with the nearest distance from sampling plot to the river. Only carabid FD responded significantly to percentage cover of vegetation productivity classes, showing a positive correlation with the proportion of medium vegetation productivity. Furthermore, overall carabid FD declined with increasing tree canopy cover. 4. Our results can help predicting spatial patterns of ground beetles according to landscape diversity and proportions of surrounding vegetation types and improve the design of conservation strategies (such as altering canopy cover) of carabids, especially forest specialist species. Any forest management strategies for promoting carabid diversity should consider the pervasive effects of landscape composition and configuration besides local stand characteristics.

Carabid abundance, species diversity and functional diversity (FD) are likely to influence the provision of ecosystem services, and these broad characteristics can be used to assess the multi-scale drivers of ground beetle assemblages (Woodcock et al., 2010; Spake et al., 2016; Philpott et al., 2019). Study on the effects of environmental factors on carabid biodiversity has traditionally utilised a taxonomic approach by focusing on their abundance or species richness (Batary et al., 2008; Fountain-Jones et al., 2015). But functional-trait analysis has several advantages over taxonomic approach in predicting various ecosystem functions and services (Kleyer et al., 2012; Fountain-Jones et al., 2015; Magura, 2017). FD captures the relative value, range or dispersion of functional traits in a community (Petchey & Gaston, 2002, 2006; Woodcock et al., 2014; Gallé et al., 2019). Thus, it is increasingly used as a metric to evaluate the responses of ground beetles to environmental change (Pavoine & Bonsall, 2011; Spake et al., 2016).

Here, we investigate how ground beetle activity density, species diversity and FD respond to stand characteristics (e.g. vegetation cover, tree canopy cover and the nearest distance from sampling plot to the river) and landscape structure of surrounding vegetation in 40 forest stands growing in natural poplar forests along the Irtysh River in Northwestern China. We used the overall diversity and percentage cover of vegetation productivity classes in buffers of 300 m radius surrounding all sampling plots as proxies for landscape structure of surrounding vegetation. Spe cifically, we hypothesised that (i) activity density of ground beetles would respond primarily to overall diversity of vegetation types in surrounding landscape, as many of them are highly mobile generalist predators and thus would benefit from different prey resources within forest landscapes; (ii) species diversity of ground beetles would also be higher in forest landscapes with higher diversity of vegetation types based on the ‘habitat heterogeneity hypothesis’ (Tews et al., 2004); and (iii) ground beetle FD would show a greater dependence on landscape structure of surrounding vegetation than local stand factors, a response that is attributed to their high mobility needed for movement between dynamically variable habitat types (Woodcock et al., 2010).

Three ecological traits that characterised functional diversity between ground beetle species included: body size (large vs. small), feeding trait (carnivorous vs. omnivorous), and wing morphology (macropterous vs. brachypterous) (Homburg et al., 2014) (Supporting Information Table S1). Body length was used as a measure of body size, which was measured as the distance from the tip of the mandibles to the end of the abdomen. Carabid species with an average body size equal to or longer than 15 mm were considered large; otherwise, they were considered small (Gobbi et al., 2007). Carabid species were considered carnivorous if they were strictly predators during their life cycle, whereas species that were occasional predators or herbivores were considered omnivorous (Gobbi & Fontaneto, 2008). For wing morphology, macropterous species were those with wings longer than the elytra, whereas brachypterous species were those with wings shorter than the elytra (Brambilla & Gobbi, 2014). Carabid FD was measured by calculating Rao’s quadratic entropy $( \mathrm { F D } _ { \mathrm { Q } } )$ , which is a multi-trait FD metric that describes the diversity of a given community, combining the relative abundances of species with the biological information about the functional differences between species (Rao, 1982; Ricotta, 2005). $\mathrm { F D } _ { \mathbf { Q } }$ expresses the average functional dissimilarity between two randomly selected individuals if relative abundance is calculated from the number of individuals, and it has been widespread used to characterise human impacts on ecosystem processes (Aubin et al., 2013). We calculated $\mathrm { F D } _ { \mathbf { Q } }$ for each sampling plot as: $\mathrm { F D { Q } = \sum } { i = 1 } ^ { S } \sum { j = 1 } ^ { S } d { i j } p { i } p { j }$ where S is the number of species in a sampling plot, $d _ { i j }$ is the dissimilarity in trait values between each species pair i and $j ,$ and

Landscape structure of surrounding vegetation was measured in a 300 m radius buffer (Wang et al., 2019). The geographical coordinates of the centre of each sampling plot were collected using a handheld GPS unit. Then, based on these coordinates, open-access remote sensing images were acquired on 28 June 2018 for the whole study area covering six villages from the European ‘Sentinel-2A’ satellite. We preprocessed remote sensing images using ENVI version 5.4 software in order to eliminate errors and improve their quality, including radiation correction and atmospheric correction. The results of image-interpretation were rectified by adequate ground-truth data recorded in a forest vegetation survey. The normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) is often used as a preferred surrogate for vegetation productivity of the terrestrial ecosystems (Voepel et al., 2011; Lezama et $a l .$ , 2014), particularly in applications involving land-cover change. Vegetation productivity was thus quantified by calculating NDVI values, which is defined as: $\mathrm{NDVI} = \left( \mathrm{R_{NIR}} - \mathrm{R_{red}} \right) / \left( \mathrm{R_{NIR}} + \mathrm{R_{red}} \right)$ , where R NIR and $\mathbf { R _ { r e d } }$ refer to the reflectance values derived from spectral radiances measured by the near-infrared channel and the red visible channel, respectively. NDVI values range from 1 (water) to 1 (maximum vegetation signal). We calculated NDVI values for each of 300 m radius buffers around sampling plots using ‘Band Math’ tool in ENVI version 5.4 software applied to the remote sensing image and classified NDVI values into five vegetation classes representing the intensity of the vegetation signal: (i) low vegetation (1.00 to 0.11); (ii) medium-low vegetation (0.11–0.21); (iii medium vegetation (0.21–0.51); (iv) medium-high vegetation (0.51–0.81); and (vi) high vegetation signal (0.81–1.00) (Fig. 1c). We distinguished each vegetation class based on a variation range examination of how NDVI values change in each habitat type (e.g. bare ground, shrubland, grassland, woodland, or farmland) across time. These vegetation productivity classes defined different habitat patches that had similar vegetation growth characteristics, for instance, NDVI values below 0.2 typically represent very low vegetation signal or bare ground. Using five classes enabled us to separate the amount of each vegetation productivity class during the growing season precisely (Macfadyen et al., 2015). Finally, the proportion of each of the five vegetation productivity classes was calculated in a buffer of 300 m radius centred on each sampling plot. Shannon’s Diversity Index (SHDI) was also calculated by using Fragstats version 4.2 to quantify the overall diversity of vegetation productivity classes.

At each sampling plot, the activity density and species richness data of ground beetles from the five pitfall traps on each transect and for the two sampling years were pooled for statistical analyses. The responses of carabid species diversity and FD to landscape structure of surrounding vegetation and stand characteristics were assessed using linear mixed-effect models (LMMs) for each response variable. The ‘lmer’ function (R package lme4; Bates et al., 2015) were used for species diversity of ground beetles, represented by the Shannon-Wiener’s diversity index (H 0 ) (function ‘diversity’ in R package vegan; Oksanen et al., 2019) and FD of ground beetles $( \mathrm { F D } _ { \mathrm { Q } } )$ as they are continuous responses. We tested the effects of stand level and landscape factors on carabid activity density using generalised linear mixed-effect models (GLMMs) with a negative binomial distribution (function ‘glmer.nb’ in R package lme4; Bates et al., 2015) since overdispersion was detected (overdispersion test via R package qcc; Scrucca, 2014). For variable selection, we conducted Spearman’s correlation test to check for correlations among the proportions of five vegetation productivity classes, the SHDI and all stand characteristics. There was a strong correlation between the DBH and canopy cover, and the latter has previously been observed to affect ground beetle assemblages in forests (Lange et al., 2014; Negro et al., 2014; Spake et al., 2016), thus DBH was not considered to be an explanatory variable for further analyses. Additionally, as species richness and average height of herbaceous plant species, the proportions of low and medium-low vegetation productivity showed a strong correlation (correlation coefficients > j0.7j) with other explanatory variables (Supporting Information Table S2), we excluded them from further analyses (Yang et al., 2019). Significant positive effect of the overall diversity of vegetation productivity classes on carabid activity density did support our first hypothesis that activity density of ground beetles would respond primarily to landscape structure of surrounding vegetation. Vele et al. (2011) investigating the effects of local site conditions and landscape factors on ant and carabid community composition in a spruce forest, found that a greater quantity of suitable habitat in the surrounding landscape increased the probability of greater abundance of carabids in both optimal and suboptimal patches, similar to our result. Additionally, species diversity of ground beetles responded strongly to stand characteristics, supporting the results of a research aimed to examine the influence of natural areas on carabid communities, which found that environmental factors at both local and landscape scales influenced ground beetle diversity and community composition (Werling & Gratton, 2008). Vele et al. (2011) also indicated that carabid community composition was strongly affected by both local conditions near the pitfall traps and the availability of optimal habitat in the surrounding landscape. In this study, at the local scale, vegetation cover and the nearest distance from sampling plot to the river were found to be the two most influential stand characteristics for carabid species diversity. Vegetation cover and distance from running/ standing water are known to be the main determinants of carabid beetle fauna (Magagula, 2003). Several previous studies suggested that species diversity of carabid beetles had a strong relationship with local habitat factors, and vegetation cover was found to be the most influential local factor for increasing carabid species diversity (Niemelä et al., 2002; Rahman et al., 2015). Vegetation cover can modify microclimatic conditions and provide ideal living space to promote the community establishment of carabid beetles and thus increase diversity of different carabid species (Rahman et al., 2015). Schlegel & Riesen (2012) also showed that high vegetation cover turned out to be the crucial habitat factor for carabid species composition and diversity. Furthermore, riparian border, a habitat with higher vegetation cover, was shown to have the highest species diversity of carabid species (Magagula, 2003). In riparian border, streams can change microclimate environment such as humidity and temperature of the adjacent terrestrial habitat, resulting in diverse animal communities (Lavallee & Richardson, 2010). A study on terrestrial ground beetle communities suggested that riparian habitats had a great influence in maintaining their species diversity in forests, in part because the changing microclimate in riparian border is the determining factor in habitat choices of different ground beetles (Rykken et al., 2007). Therefore, in natural poplar forest ecosystems, the higher vegetation cover can support more ground beetle species that rely on diverse microclimates of riparian habitats. This study demonstrated the potential importance of vegetation cover and the distance to the river to carabid species diversity.
